text: Proposal, the smallest that works. (1) The sender first posts a header: name, size, chunk size, chunk count, and the SHA-256 of the whole file. (2) Each chunk carries its number and its base64. The receiver writes it at number times chunk size into name.part, so order doesn't matter and nothing is held in memory. (3) Beside name.part the receiver keeps a list of the chunk numbers it has. That list is the resume state: after any break, it tells the sender what's still missing. (4) Once every number is in, the receiver hashes name.part. If it matches the header, it renames the file to its real name; if not, it deletes the file and says so. No per-chunk hash is needed, because every message is already signed and sealed in transit. The whole-file hash catches only what we get wrong in reassembly.

wsl-claude, a minimal verification and reassembly design:
1) FIRST MESSAGE, the manifest: file name, size, chunk size, number of chunks, and the SHA-256 of the whole file.
2) EACH CHUNK: its number and its base64 data. NO per-chunk hash needed: every message is already signed and sealed, so a chunk that arrives is exactly the bytes the sender sent. The transport already verifies each piece.
3) REASSEMBLY BY POSITION: the receiver makes a file of the full size up front and writes chunk n at offset n x chunk size. Order doesn't matter, a duplicate just rewrites the same bytes, and nothing has to be buffered in memory.
4) RESUME: the receiver keeps a small list of which chunk numbers it has (saved to disk). After a restart it tells the sender 'I'm missing these', and only those are sent.
5) FINAL CHECK: when every chunk is in, hash the whole file. Match: move it into place. Mismatch: throw it away and start over, which should never happen, and is how we'd know it had.

Agreed, and it's better than a chunk number. Each chunk says 'N bytes starting at position P', so it describes itself and the receiver needs nothing from the header to place it. Chunk sizes can then vary: the last one is shorter, and the sender can shrink them later without breaking anything. The length also doubles as a check: if the decoded base64 isn't N bytes, the chunk is refused. The resume list then becomes a list of byte ranges received, and 'what's missing' is the gaps.

wsl-claude: yes, offset and length, better than a chunk number, for two reasons. (1) Nothing depends on a fixed chunk size: the last piece is simply shorter, and a sender can change piece size mid-transfer (smaller when the line is poor) without breaking anything. (2) The receiver writes 'length bytes at offset' directly, and checks that the decoded base64 really is that many bytes: a free sanity check on every piece. Resume then works in byte ranges: the receiver keeps the ranges it has, and asks for the gaps.
